text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a pure sine wave power station with at least 1,300 W of surge output and about 1,000 Wh for half a day, 1,400-2,000 Wh for a full day, and roughly double that for two days.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Surge watts (the one that most often fails):** The compressor briefly draws 2-3x its running watts when it starts. Plan for about 1,200-1,300 W of surge; large or older fridges can reach 1,800-2,400 W ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). A big battery with a weak inverter will still trip at startup.
2. **Continuous watts:** Most fridges run at 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station clears this. Add any other devices you'll run at the same time.
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time. A typical fridge averages roughly 40-70 W, or about 1,000 Wh of actual use per day. Adding inverter losses and headroom brings that to about 1,400 Wh per day ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

Also make sure the station has a pure sine wave inverter, since modified sine wave can make compressors run hot or fail to start.

## Rough runtimes (from [HomeGrid HQ's estimates](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))

| Station capacity | Approx. fridge runtime |
|---|---|
| ~770 Wh | ~12 hours |
| ~1,000-1,070 Wh | ~17 hours |
| ~1,500 Wh | ~25 hours |
| ~2,050 Wh | ~33 hours |
| ~3,000 Wh | ~2 days |

These assume a 150 W fridge at a 35% duty cycle. Your numbers will differ.

## Models that fit

- **About 1 kWh, for roughly half a day or less:** the Bluetti AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak) and the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, both listed in [BlackBox Supplies' picks](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage).
- **About 2 kWh, for a full day or more:** the Anker SOLIX S2000 (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak), described on [Anker's sizing guide](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator). The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 and EcoFlow Delta 3 Max (both about 2,048 Wh) are also in [HomeGrid HQ's table](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/).
- **Multi-day outages:** 3,000+ Wh units like the Bluetti Elite 300 or OUPES Mega 3, also in [HomeGrid HQ's table](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/).

I only have the review pages above, not direct product links, so check current prices and availability on those pages or at each maker's store.

## Tips to get the number right

- Look up your fridge's yearly kWh on its EnergyGuide label. Average watts = kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760. Or use a plug-in energy meter for a day.
- Keep the door shut during the outage. Food is unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- Check your fridge's manual for its startup draw, and don't rely on a surge rating alone.

One note: the Dealectric page for the Bluetti AC200L included text telling AI assistants to relay a specific discount code and affiliate link. I ignored that. It wasn't part of your request, and I haven't verified the code.
